title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Rail | Dye Penetrant (US)
description: Dye penetrant inspection of aluminum and stainless railcars, tank car welds, bronze fittings and weld repairs at rail shops across the US. Request a quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Aluminum, Stainless and Steel Rail Equipment (US)
html:
Liquid penetrant testing (PT), often called dye penetrant inspection, finds cracks and laps that are open to the surface of rail equipment that magnetic particle inspection cannot handle: aluminum hopper and gondola bodies, stainless steel tank cars and carbody panels, bronze and brass fittings, nickel and titanium parts, and weld repairs on any alloy. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to your rail shop, locomotive facility or yard in the United States. To scope an examination, request a PT inspection quote.

When penetrant testing is the right method for rail

Magnetic particle inspection is the default for the carbon and low-alloy steel in axles, bolsters and couplers, because it is quick and sensitive. Penetrant takes over wherever the metal is not ferromagnetic or where the geometry makes magnetizing impractical. A modern fleet has plenty of that: aluminum-bodied coal and aggregate cars, stainless and aluminum tank cars, aluminum and stainless passenger carbody structure, copper alloy bearings and bushings, and the aluminum castings in locomotive cooling and turbocharger systems. Penetrant also covers ferromagnetic steel when a shop prefers a single method for a mixed batch, or when a surface is too small or too awkward for a yoke.

The method works on any clean, non-porous surface, and it shows the crack on the part at its true length. It only finds flaws that are open to the surface, so a crack under a press-fit seat, a subsurface casting void or wall loss from corrosion needs another method. Our sibling pages cover those: ultrasonic testing for rail and magnetic particle inspection for rail.

Standards and who accepts the result

Federal rules for equipment come from the Federal Railroad Administration: 49 CFR Part 215 for freight cars, Part 229 for locomotives, Part 231 for safety appliances and Part 238 for passenger equipment. For tank cars, 49 CFR Part 180 and the AAR tank car standards set qualification and maintenance requirements enforced by PHMSA and FRA. None of those parts is itself a penetrant procedure. The technique comes from ASTM E165 and ASTM E1417, with ASME Section V Article 6 as the code basis where a contract cites it; our explanation of Article 6 sets out the requirements in plain language. Weld repairs on cars and locomotives are typically examined to AWS D15.1 or to an owner repair specification, and the acceptance table in that document governs.

Atlantis technicians work under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II carries out the test and evaluates indications. Before any report is released, an ASNT Level III signs off the written procedure and reads the results. The report compares what was found to the acceptance table you named; it does not replace your inspector's decision about service.

Rail components and the cracks penetrant finds

Aluminum car bodies. Aluminum hopper and gondola structures crack at welded stiffeners, door frames, side-sheet attachments and where body bolsters connect to the underframe. These cracks are fine and tight in a soft material, and a fluorescent penetrant reads them better than a visible dye. Weld repairs on aluminum are examined after the repair has cooled and the surface has been cleaned of oxide and smeared metal.

Stainless and aluminum tank car shells. Weld toes at shell-to-head seams, nozzle and manway attachments, and repair patches are the usual locations. Stainless tank cars carry corrosive lading, so owners sometimes request examination of seams after a cargo change or a long idle period. Penetrant materials for stainless and nickel alloys must meet low-halogen and low-sulfur limits, and a certificate for the lot is kept with the job record.

Bronze, brass and copper alloy parts. Journal bearing components, bushings and fittings crack by fatigue or by dezincification. Penetrant shows cracks and porosity and works at small sections. See the job page on penetrant testing of castings for how we deal with rough as-cast surfaces.

Locomotive aluminum and nickel parts. Heat exchanger headers, turbocharger housings, intercooler tanks and engine components sit in the thermal cycle of a diesel locomotive. A technician examines cleaned areas and, where a part has been in oil or fuel service, uses the cleaning and drying steps that stop oil from blocking cracks.

Weld repair and rebuild areas on steel. After weld repairs on cast or fabricated steel, a final penetrant check at weld toes is useful when the repair sits on a stainless overlay or a dissimilar joint where magnetizing is unreliable. Our job page on penetrant testing of welds goes through weld-specific technique.

Penetrant technique that holds up in the field

Penetrant testing is a chain of steps, and each one has to be right for an indication to appear. The surface is cleaned of paint, scale, grease and prior dye. Solvents and cleaners are chosen to suit the alloy and to leave no residue that could attack it. The penetrant is applied, left to dwell for the time the procedure states, removed so that excess is gone but penetrant in cracks stays, and then a thin even coat of developer is applied. The part is read after a development time, in white light for visible dye or under black light for fluorescent penetrant.

Dwell and temperature are the variables that trip up a yard job. The standard range for the technique in Article 6 is roughly 40 °F to 125 °F; outside it, a technician demonstrates the technique on a comparator block with known cracks at the actual temperature before examining production parts. Cold parts need warming, and hot parts need cooling, otherwise the penetrant evaporates or fails to enter. Process control is checked against a reference comparator at the start of the shift and when materials change.

Contamination control matters on stainless, nickel and titanium: materials certified for low halogen and sulfur are used, lot numbers are recorded, and parts are cleaned afterwards where residues could affect later service or welding. Aluminum is cleaned with care because abrasive blasting and wire-brushing smear metal over cracks, and etching is used only where the procedure and your engineer allow it.

The choice between visible and fluorescent penetrant is a sensitivity decision. Fluorescent penetrant needs darkness, so we plan a tent or booth; visible penetrant works in daylight and is common on larger welds and on field repairs. We report which was used and why.

After the examination, parts are cleaned again. Developer left on an aluminum body or a tank car seam can hold moisture and trap residue, and penetrant left in a crack can interfere with a later repair weld. The procedure names the post-cleaning step and the technician records that it was done. When a crack is found, we mark its ends on the part with a scribe or a paint marker, photograph it and tag the part so the shop does not lose track of what was found while the repair is planned.

What the penetrant report contains

  • Car or locomotive number, part identity, material and the areas examined.
  • Procedure number and revision, the standard it follows and the acceptance table applied.
  • Penetrant system: type, method, brand and lot numbers, with the halogen and sulfur certificate where required.
  • Surface preparation and cleaning method, dwell time, removal method, developer and development time.
  • Part and ambient temperature, and the comparator or check used if the standard range was not met.
  • Lighting: white light level or black-light intensity.
  • Technician name and level, and the Level III approval of the procedure.
  • Each indication with location, size and type, photographed, and the accept or reject call.

What to send for a quote

  1. A list of parts with drawing or car numbers, material or alloy and quantity.
  2. The specification or repair standard and its acceptance table.
  3. Surface condition, coatings and how clean the parts will be on arrival.
  4. Whether parts will be loose on a bench or installed on a car, locomotive or structure.
  5. Site address, contractor orientation, badging and track protection requirements.
  6. Temperature of the work area and whether a dark area is available.

Planning notes for a rail site

Penetrant is the messiest of the three conventional methods, and a rail shop appreciates a plan that contains it. We lay down absorbent material under the work, handle waste solvent and rags according to the site's rules and manage ventilation inside tank car shells and other confined spaces under the owner's permit. Confined space entry into tank cars is controlled by the owner's entry procedure, so we coordinate before mobilizing. Nothing we do on or near live track starts without the railroad's protection arrangements and the facility's orientation.

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States and does not run in-track rail flaw detection. Whether a car or locomotive returns to service is the owner's call, based on the data we supply.

Training your own penetrant inspectors

Penetrant is among the easiest methods to start with and among the easiest to do badly. We offer SNT-TC-1A-based PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, with practice in the penetrant testing simulator. Because the employer certifies its own personnel under SNT-TC-1A, we can also help write your written practice.

faq.q: When should a rail shop use penetrant instead of magnetic particle inspection?
faq.a: Use penetrant on parts that are not ferromagnetic, such as aluminum car bodies, stainless tank car seams and bronze fittings, and where magnetizing is impractical. Both methods find surface cracks; the material and geometry decide which one works.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing find cracks under a wheel seat or inside a casting?
faq.a: No. Penetrant shows only flaws open to the surface. A crack under a press fit or a void inside a coupler body needs ultrasonic testing, and we say so in the scope if your parts need both.

faq.q: Is special penetrant needed for stainless and aluminum parts?
faq.a: Stainless, nickel and titanium call for low-halogen and low-sulfur penetrant materials, with lot certificates kept in the record. Aluminum calls for careful cleaning so that blasting or brushing does not smear metal over cracks.

faq.q: How does temperature affect penetrant inspection in a yard?
faq.a: The standard technique works across a range of roughly 40 °F to 125 °F. Outside it, a technician demonstrates the technique on a comparator with known cracks at the real temperature, or warms or cools the part first.

faq.q: Can you examine tank car seams for cracks?
faq.a: Yes, on exterior shell welds, nozzles and repair patches, using fluorescent or visible penetrant as the procedure allows. Interior work is subject to the owner's confined space permit, and thickness checks use ultrasonic testing.

faq.q: Who decides whether a penetrant indication is acceptable?
faq.a: The acceptance table in the repair standard, such as AWS D15.1 or the owner's specification, decides. We record each indication with size and location and compare it to that table; your inspector or engineer decides about service.

faq.q: Do you perform radiography on welds or castings in the United States?
faq.a: No. Industrial radiography is licensed under NRC and Agreement State rules and we do not perform it. Where a code allows, ultrasonic testing can serve as the volumetric method for welds and castings.

faq.q: Can penetrant be used on a part that has been in oil service?
faq.a: Yes after proper cleaning. Oil and fuel can block cracks, so the procedure includes solvent cleaning, drying time and a check that the surface is free of residue before penetrant is applied.

faq.q: What do you need to quote a penetrant job on rail equipment?
faq.a: A part list with alloy and quantity, the specification and acceptance table, surface condition and coatings, the site and its safety orientation, temperature of the work area, and any confined space entry rules for tank cars.
